extracted.intended_audience: general readers and practitioners interested in TV political satire (SNL writers/performers, fans of sketch comedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and implicit standards for producing and performing political impressions on TV sketch shows, with emphasis on truth‑based 'fair hits', accurate mimicry, careful preparation, and awareness of impact. Draws on Tina Fey's comments about her Sarah Palin impression and other SNL political work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair hit (truth-based satire)
rubrics_metrics.description: “We always worked really hard to make sure they were what we call a ‘fair hit.’ It only felt like it would work if it was based in something that was true.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire should be rooted in verifiable truth about the subject — a joke should exaggerate or expose something real rather than inventing false attributes. The article uses Fey’s Palin impression as an example of a 'fair hit.' Antipattern: relying on falsehoods or invented traits that make the joke landless or unfair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of impression/performance
rubrics_metrics.description: “He came in and just played him so perfectly... It only works if it’s correct.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impersonations should capture recognizable, factual details of the target (voice, mannerisms, documented behavior) so the audience immediately recognizes and accepts the caricature. Example: Matt Damon’s Brett Kavanaugh impression 'worked' because it reflected the real-life context (e.g., Kavanaugh 'did like beer').

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous preparation and craft
rubrics_metrics.description: “We always worked really hard to make sure they were what we call a ‘fair hit.’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producing effective political comedy requires effort, research, and careful crafting — not just a quick punchline. Writers/performers should vet jokes against facts and test whether the premise genuinely reflects the subject. Scoring note: effort and research are presented as prerequisites for a successful sketch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of impact and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is fascinating to know that what you say will be taken seriously... it’s a thrilling and almost scary thing to have this idea that something you say will be heard by the person in charge.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comics and writers should be mindful that their material may be heard by powerful figures and can influence public perception; this implies an ethical responsibility to avoid careless harm. Fey acknowledges regretting some jokes ('I was on the wrong side of that'), illustrating the expectation of reflection and accountability when a joke misfires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not aim to 'control the narrative' — reflect rather than manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: In response to 'Does SNL try to control the narrative of politics?' Fey said, 'And they really do not.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The stated principle is that successful political satire reflects and amplifies existing truths rather than attempting to manufacture or steer political narratives. Antipattern: creating sketches whose primary purpose is to manipulate political outcomes rather than to comment on observed realities.
